defects.description: The design claims cross-AZ availability but gives only one subnet placement for the ALB and EKS, with no worker-node or pod distribution specified. Explicitly document load-balancer subnet associations, worker capacity in both AZs, replica placement and disruption handling; the datastore multiAz flags do not establish compute resilience.

R9 calls for an ingress controller, but none is identified. Specify the controller, Kubernetes Service/Ingress resources, target registration and certificate provisioning rather than leaving ALB-to-EKS routing as an unexplained integration.

Private placement and datastore encryption are useful, but workload IAM permissions, database credentials, security-group restrictions and database/cache transport encryption are not specified. Define service-level access boundaries and secret handling before implementation.

CloudWatch and X-Ray are destinations rather than a complete telemetry implementation. Identify log collectors, metric collection, application trace instrumentation/exporters, retention settings and actionable alarms.

The private-subnet design does not show how workloads reach container registries, telemetry endpoints or other required external dependencies. Document the intended outbound connectivity and its behavior during an AZ failure.

reviews.summary: The service choices fit the Kubernetes migration, but compute HA and implementation details remain unresolved; documentation-dependent findings throughout this review are conservatively rated minor because official AWS documentation could not be checked.

defects.description: The SNS-to-app HTTPS arrow leaves native push delivery underspecified. Identify the mobile push provider integration, platform application/endpoints, device-token registration and lifecycle, and recipient-specific subscriptions or publishing; clarify that the arrow represents logical delivery rather than an unexplained phone HTTPS subscription.

The direct upload is labelled presigned, but no authenticated URL-issuance operation is shown. Specify how the backend authorizes the upload, chooses an owner-scoped object key, limits URL lifetime and permissions, and keeps photos private.

The only database operation shown is saving a workout. The design does not explain friendship queries, trusted record comparisons, recipient selection, per-user data authorization or concurrent record updates, which are necessary to determine whose record was beaten and whom to notify.

Workout persistence and notification publication share one request-processing function without a stated recovery contract. Define request idempotency, handling of publication failure after a successful save, notification retries and failure capture, plus alarms for failed requests and delivery.

The design does not explicitly select DynamoDB on-demand capacity or settle the peak-traffic assumption. Document the billing mode, expected burst envelope, throttling/retry behavior and retention/lifecycle decisions so pay-per-use and New Year readiness are implementation choices rather than general service descriptions.

reviews.summary: The serverless service selection suits spiky mobile traffic, but native push delivery, authorized photo uploads and friend-record processing remain insufficiently specified.

reviews.summary: The managed serverless foundation matches the operating model, but the upload, native push and friend-record workflows need implementation-level decisions before deployment.

defects.description: Per-device certificates are specified, but device authorization and lifecycle controls are not. Define certificate provisioning/revocation, device-scoped topic permissions, least-privilege rule and processor permissions, and how the processor binds the reading's device identity to an authenticated publisher rather than trusting an arbitrary payload identifier.

The ingestion function combines registry lookup, persistence and SMS publication without explicit retry, failure-capture or idempotency behavior. Specify the IoT routing rule and recovery path, prevent duplicate readings/alerts on retries, and add alarms for ingestion failures, processing backlog and SMS delivery problems.

The Cognito-to-API JWT edge obscures the actual token flow. Show the dashboard obtaining a token and sending it with API requests, and specify the HTTP API authorizer's issuer, audience and claim handling rather than leaving 'Cognito' as the complete configuration.

The 90-day window appears in purpose statements but not an explicit retention configuration. Define retention and deletion behavior, device/time query filtering, aggregation and pagination; one device produces 129,600 readings in 90 days, so an unrestricted raw-history response should not be the only dashboard query shape.

The fleet produces 72 million readings per day, yet the design gives no throughput or cost assumptions for per-reading Lambda execution, registry lookup and storage. Define acceptable repeated-alert behavior, SMS budgets and spending/delivery controls so prolonged out-of-range conditions do not create an uncontrolled notification bill.

reviews.summary: The managed ingestion, ownership and dashboard components cover the main use cases, but device authorization, recovery, explicit retention and high-volume alert economics need further definition.

preference.why: Both select the same appropriate services and share the same unresolved compute-HA and implementation details; moving the Redis node's depicted placement between AZs does not establish a different resilience design when both specify multiAz.

The architectures and integration gaps are materially identical; A states somewhat clearer retention and preprocessing assumptions, but neither resolves native push delivery, presigned URL issuance or friend-record processing.

Both implement the same ingestion, registry, storage, authorization and notification flows and share the same operational gaps; A's additional registry encryption annotation does not establish a materially different architecture.
